title: Audit logs & admin activity review - Glacier Bank
summary: Redwood walked Glacier Bank through audit logging and admin activity capture: what events are recorded, export/streaming options (S3/Kinesis/Splunk/webhook), retention defaults and enterprise options, KMS encryption and key access patterns, RBAC/SSO interactions, and compliance alignment (SOC 2/ISO). Customer requested log schema and a short trial stream to their test Splunk instance. Next steps agreed: share log schema + SOC2 certs, setup a 2-week streaming pilot, and schedule SE deep-dive for retention/archival policy.
topics: export and streaming options: S3, Kinesis, Splunk, webhooks
RBAC and SSO interaction with logs

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:30 PST
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood CSM), Olivia Park (Glacier Bank CISO), Mark Rivera (Infra), Sara Lin (Compliance), Tommy Vu (App Sec)

Summary (auto): quick run through of audit logs and admin activity capture; confirm export destinations, retention options, KMS integration, and compliance artifacts. Client asks for sample logs and trial stream.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh let's do quick intros, um and we'll focus on audit logging and admin activity capture for your private deployment and hosted usage, ok?
[00:18] Olivia: yeah thanks Maya, we just want to confirm what gets captured, how long you keep it, and how we can export into our Splunk and S3 buckets. Also KMS questions.
[00:30] Ethan: great; quick note, for context we typically capture both platform-level and admin-level events; I'll run through the event categories and then we'll show export options.
[00:45] Mark: ok, and high level - we're doing private deployment in GCP, but some teams might use hosted, so retention and routing matters.
[00:55] Maya: perfect. Ethan, take it away.
[01:02] Ethan: sure. So we log: authentication events (SSO sign-ins, token/refreshes), user management (invites, role changes, RBAC updates), admin actions (model rollouts, config changes, VPC and network config updates), API key lifecycle (create, revoke, rotate), billing-ish events (quota changes), and runtime operational events (node scale, pod restarts) — also request metadata like source IP, user-agent, request id, timestamp.
[01:30] Ethan: we try to capture the who, the what, the when and where — so who's acting, what they changed, the object id, the previous and new value where applic — sometimes payloads are truncated for privacy.
[01:44] Olivia: and do you capture request payloads? Like prompt content? We need to be careful with banking PII.
[01:52] Ethan: good question. For hosted API by default we do not log full prompt bodies in audit logs; we capture metadata and a request hash. For dedicated/private deployments we can configure to scrub or not collect prompt content; and we support prefix/KV cache logs as separate optional debug traces but those are off by default.
[02:10] Sara: so for compliance we need assurance that logs aren't editable and are retained for at least two years for certain datasets. Do you offer immutability or WORM?
[02:20] Ethan: yes — enterprise plans can enable immutable archival to customer-owned S3 with WORM policies or we can write to a retention bucket with object lock. We also support event signing for tamper evidence.
[02:35] Tommy: and about encryption — our security team wants customer-managed keys. How does Redwood integrate with KMS/HSM?
[02:41] Maya: quick answer: we support customer-managed keys for both at-rest storage of logs and for encrypting the control plane data. We integrate with cloud KMS (GCP KMS, AWS KMS) and we have an HSM option for private deployments. Ethan?
[02:52] Ethan: yep, logs at rest can be encrypted with a customer KMS; we only store the key reference — key material remains in your KMS. For streaming to S3 we can sign objects server-side with your key or leave it for you to re-encrypt on arrival.
[03:10] Mark: what about access — who in Redwood can access these logs? We need RBAC and a clear audit trail of Redwood access for support.
[03:19] Maya: support access is limited and require explicit request; all access is logged as well. We have RBAC for Redwood staff and customers; you can choose support roles that are read-only.
[03:30] Ethan: and every time a Redwood engineer accesses a customer's logs, that's an auditable event captured in the same audit stream with justification and ticket id.
[03:40] Olivia: good. Export formats? We prefer streaming into Splunk HEC and long-term in S3.
[03:46] Ethan: supported sinks: S3 (JSON newline), Kinesis or Pub/Sub, Splunk HEC, Syslog, webhooks to SIEM, and direct API pull. We also support periodic bulk exports for archives.
[04:05] Sara: can we restrict retention per event type? For ex, auth events 2 years, operational logs 90 days?
[04:12] Ethan: yes — retention is configurable by event class. Defaults: 90 days for most operational logs, 365 for admin/audit by default on enterprise plans we can do custom like 2 years, or send to your archival S3 with object lock.
[04:30] Speaker 1: (mumble) default something something 90 days yeah
[04:36] Maya: also there's hot indexing for 30 days so you can search quickly, and then cold storage for longer retention.
[04:45] Mark: search and query options? We want to be able to pull by user, ip, action, timeframe.
[04:51] Ethan: console has an events explorer with filters by actor, action, object id, ip, timeframe; we also include a raw JSON download for each event and you can export query results to S3.
[05:05] Olivia: any chance to stream to our SIEM and have near real-time alerting?
[05:11] Ethan: yes Splunk HEC and syslog are near-real-time; throughput depends on your load — we have buffering and backpressure, and for large volumes we recommend Kinesis or Pub/Sub as a durable buffer.
[05:25] Sara: compliance evidence — can we get attestations and logs for audits?
[05:30] Maya: we can provide SOC 2 Type II reports, ISO attestations and map specific log samples to evidence. We'll redact any customer PII per policy.
[05:40] Olivia: ok good. A few nitty-gritty questions: do you include IP geolocation, and do you store user-agent strings?
[05:48] Ethan: yes both included. IP and user agent are stored as metadata and available in the event JSON. We also store request ids for cross-correlation.
[05:58] Tommy: how about API key logs — if a key is exfiltrated can we see which requests used it and then invalidate?
[06:05] Ethan: every request includes the key id in the event; you can search and immediately revoke key which will be an admin event. We also retain an index of recent key usage for quick triage.
[06:20] Mark: what about model rollout logs — we need to track who promoted a model version and when and what variant was used.
[06:27] Ethan: exactly — model rollouts, canary steps, and fallback triggers are recorded with before/after state and can be exported as part of the audit set.
[06:38] Maya: quick note: sometimes the transcript here will show redwood product names slightly off in the auto transcription — ignore that.
[06:45] Olivia: hah, noted.
[06:48] Sara: any limits to log retention on hosted tiers? We don't want surprises where logs are auto-deleted after 30 days.
[06:55] Maya: hosted free tiers have 30-90 days depending on plan; enterprise has configurable retention. We'll put this in the pricing doc.
[07:05] Olivia: For the pilot we want 2 years for admin logs and 90 days for infra logs. Can you support exporting to our S3 with object lock?
[07:12] Ethan: yes — we can stream to your S3 with object lock enabled; we'll coordinate with your infra to ensure bucket policy and cross-account role is correct.
[07:22] Mark: who sets the retention? The console or an API?
[07:27] Ethan: both. You can set retention rules in the console UI or via the management API.
[07:32] Tommy: is there a way to get real-time alerts when an admin role is granted?
[07:37] Ethan: yes we support alerting rules against the audit stream — you can hook to PagerDuty or webhook to your SIEM and fire alerts on role changes, or suspicious sign-ins.
[07:47] Olivia: about PII — how do you handle prompt data if someone inadvertently sends bank info?
[07:52] Ethan: again, prompt bodies are not stored in standard audit logs; if you enable debug traces they can contain sample data but we recommend scrubbing. We also offer automated redaction rules by pattern (SSNs, account numbers) for debug traces.
[08:05] Speaker 2: (uh) that redaction is regex based, some customers want more...
[08:10] Sara: can we get an SLA that logs will be available for X days and a guarantee on retention?
[08:16] Maya: retention SLA is part of enterprise contracts; we can include uptime for the log search and guarantees for exports. We'll include language in the enterprise addendum.
[08:26] Olivia: ok, let's talk about proof of concept — we want to run a 2-week streaming pilot into Splunk and verify schema and retention.
[08:33] Maya: great. We'll need a test endpoint and a service account. Ethan can help set up event filters so you only get audit and admin events.
[08:42] Ethan: I'll also run a quick demo of the event JSON and show how to map Splunk fields.
[08:48] Mark: about logs for support access — want to be sure every support access has a ticket id and reason in the log.
[08:54] Ethan: that's standard for enterprise, we capture support access with a ticket ref; it's enforced via our access workflows.
[09:00] Olivia: any query limits for the console? We have massive logs, need to run long queries.
[09:06] Ethan: long-running queries are allowed but we throttle; for heavy analysis we recommend exporting query results to S3 and running offline analysis or using your SIEM.
[09:16] Maya: let's recap next steps. We'll send the schema, SOC docs, and set up the Splunk pilot. Ethan will schedule the deep technical dive. Jordan will send retention pricing.
[09:28] Olivia: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[09:31] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts in the thread.

(End of transcript)
